claim: Memory consolidation occurs both at the scale of individual cells (cellular consolidation), which happens in the order of seconds to hours, and at the scale of brain networks (systems consolidation), which takes place in the days to weeks after learning.
source: Memory consolidation occurs both at the scale of individual cells (cellular consolidation), which happens in the order of seconds to hours, and at the scale of brain networks (systems consolidation), which takes place in the days to weeks after learning (Dudai, 2004; Dudai, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dudai 2004 and Dudai 2012, which are referenced works in the field.

claim: Systems consolidation across several brain areas is thought to be essential for the establishment of enduring memories.
source: Systems consolidation across several brain areas is thought to be essential for the establishment of enduring memories (Nadel and Hardt, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nadel and Hardt 2011.

claim: The hippocampus was demonstrated to be necessary during the early stages of memory formation and the retrieval of recent memories.
source: Traditionally, the hippocampus (HPC) was demonstrated to be necessary during the early stages of memory formation and the retrieval of recent memories (which in the mouse are typically studied one day after encoding), while the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) was found to be rather responsible for the consolidation and retrieval of remote memories (which are studied at least 14 days after encoding) (Albo and Gräff, 2018; Frankland and Bontempi, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Albo and Gräff 2018 and Frankland and Bontempi 2005.

claim: The medial prefrontal cortex was found to be responsible for the consolidation and retrieval of remote memories.
source: Traditionally, the hippocampus (HPC) was demonstrated to be necessary during the early stages of memory formation and the retrieval of recent memories (which in the mouse are typically studied one day after encoding), while the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) was found to be rather responsible for the consolidation and retrieval of remote memories (which are studied at least 14 days after encoding) (Albo and Gräff, 2018; Frankland and Bontempi, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Albo and Gräff 2018 and Frankland and Bontempi 2005.

claim: Multiple studies using immediate early gene mapping, whole brain region inhibition, or cell type-specific optogenetic manipulations showed that the mPFC was predominantly important at later times as opposed to the HPC.
source: Indeed, multiple studies using immediate early gene mapping (IEGs, that are expressed specifically upon neuronal activation), whole brain region inhibition, or cell type-specific optogenetic manipulations (Aceti et al., 2015; Frankland et al., 2004; Frankland et al., 2006; Goshen et al., 2011; Makino et al., 2019; Silva et al., 2019; Wheeler et al., 2013) showed that the mPFC was predominantly important at later times as opposed to the HPC.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies using various experimental techniques.

claim: Recent evidence has challenged the traditional view by highlighting a role for the mPFC during fear memory encoding.
source: However, recent evidence has challenged this view by highlighting a role for the mPFC also during fear memory encoding (Bero et al., 2014; Cho et al., 2017; Cummings and Clem, 2020; Tang et al., 2005; Zelikowsky et al., 2013) as well as for fear memory recall at recent times (Do-Monte et al., 2015; Rajasethupathy et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple recent studies.

claim: Recent evidence has highlighted a role for the mPFC for fear memory recall at recent times.
source: However, recent evidence has challenged this view by highlighting a role for the mPFC also during fear memory encoding (Bero et al., 2014; Cho et al., 2017; Cummings and Clem, 2020; Tang et al., 2005; Zelikowsky et al., 2013) as well as for fear memory recall at recent times (Do-Monte et al., 2015; Rajasethupathy et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Do-Monte et al. 2015 and Rajasethupathy et al. 2015.

claim: The mPFC receives inputs from other cortical areas, including sensory ones, as well as from various subcortical areas such as the hippocampal formation, amygdala, and thalamus.
source: The rich connectivity of the mPFC indeed places it as a potential hub region for memory consolidation, as it receives not only inputs from other cortical areas, including sensory ones, but also from various subcortical areas such as the hippocampal formation, amygdala, and thalamus (Dixsaut and Gräff, 2021; Le Merre et al., 2021), which are all implicated in memory formation (Cho et al., 2017; Nonaka et al., 2014; Ramirez et al., 2013; Reijmers et al., 2007; Taylor et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dixsaut and Gräff 2021 and Le Merre et al. 2021.

claim: The hippocampal formation, amygdala, and thalamus are all implicated in memory formation.
source: The rich connectivity of the mPFC indeed places it as a potential hub region for memory consolidation, as it receives not only inputs from other cortical areas, including sensory ones, but also from various subcortical areas such as the hippocampal formation, amygdala, and thalamus (Dixsaut and Gräff, 2021; Le Merre et al., 2021), which are all implicated in memory formation (Cho et al., 2017; Nonaka et al., 2014; Ramirez et al., 2013; Reijmers et al., 2007; Taylor et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on memory formation.

claim: Memories are encoded and stored in engram cells, which are cells that are activated during the initial learning, undergo molecular and/or cellular modifications following learning, and the reactivation of which correlates with and can trigger memory recall.
source: At the cellular level, mounting evidence suggests that memories are encoded and stored in engram cells, which, by definition (Tonegawa et al., 2015), are cells that are activated during the initial learning, undergo molecular and/or cellular modifications following learning, and the reactivation of which correlates with and can trigger memory recall.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tonegawa et al. 2015 for the definition of engram cells.

claim: Engram cells have been discovered in the hippocampus.
source: Engram cells have been discovered not only in the HPC (Josselyn et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2012; Ramirez et al., 2013), but more recently also in the mPFC (DeNardo et al., 2019; Kitamura et al., 2017; Matos et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies that discovered engram cells in the hippocampus.

claim: Engram cells have been discovered in the mPFC.
source: Engram cells have been discovered not only in the HPC (Josselyn et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2012; Ramirez et al., 2013), but more recently also in the mPFC (DeNardo et al., 2019; Kitamura et al., 2017; Matos et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent studies that discovered engram cells in the mPFC.

claim: Engram cells in the mPFC have the particular feature of staying silent until the memory is fully consolidated, although they are formed during the original learning phase.
source: Interestingly, engram cells in the mPFC were reported to have the particular feature of staying silent until the memory is fully consolidated, although they are formed during the original learning phase (DeNardo et al., 2019; Kitamura et al., 2017; Matos et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies reporting this feature of mPFC engram cells.

claim: mPFC engram cells are first active during encoding, stay silent during a recent recall, and are reactivated at remote recall.
source: This implies that mPFC engram cells are first active during encoding, stay silent during a recent recall, and are reactivated at remote recall, although they are functionally able to trigger memory retrieval at any time.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the cited studies about mPFC engram cell behavior.

claim: mPFC engram cells are functionally able to trigger memory retrieval at any time.
source: This implies that mPFC engram cells are first active during encoding, stay silent during a recent recall, and are reactivated at remote recall, although they are functionally able to trigger memory retrieval at any time.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the cited studies about mPFC engram cell functionality.

claim: The mPFC is composed of three major areas: the anterior cingulate (ACC), the prelimbic (PL), and the infralimbic (IL) cortices.
source: The mPFC is composed of the three following major areas: The anterior cingulate (ACC), the prelimbic (PL) and the infralimbic (IL) cortices (Carlén, 2017; Le Merre et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Carlén 2017 and Le Merre et al. 2021.

claim: At both recent and remote recall, mice display a significantly higher freezing percentage than the no shock control groups.
source: We observed that both at recent and remote recall, mice display a significantly higher freezing percentage than the no shock control groups (Figure 1B), indicating successful memory formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mice displaying significantly higher freezing at recent and remote recall compared to no shock controls indicates successful memory formation.
source: We observed that both at recent and remote recall, mice display a significantly higher freezing percentage than the no shock control groups (Figure 1B), indicating successful memory formation.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental data based on established knowledge about fear conditioning.

claim: All mPFC regions were more active at encoding than during the memory recalls.
source: We found that while all regions were more active at encoding than during the memory recalls, only in the PL did we observe a significant increase in cFos compared to the no shock control groups (Figure 1C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-F.

claim: Only in the PL was there a significant increase in cFos compared to the no shock control groups.
source: We found that while all regions were more active at encoding than during the memory recalls, only in the PL did we observe a significant increase in cFos compared to the no shock control groups (Figure 1C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-F.

claim: The mPFC as a whole, and the PL in particular, are activated by the encoding of a contextual fear memory.
source: These results indicate that the mPFC as a whole, and the PL in particular, are activated by the encoding of a contextual fear memory.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental data on cFos expression.

claim: The finding that the PL is activated during encoding suggests an important role of the PL during this early phase of memory consolidation.
source: In turn, this finding suggests an important role of the PL already during this early phase of memory consolidation, which is coherent with the formation of engram cells in the PL at the time of encoding (DeNardo et al., 2019; Kitamura et al., 2017; Matos et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data, supported by citations to studies on PL engram cells.

claim: Tamoxifen injection increased the number of starter cells expressing both GFP and mCherry in PL compared to vehicle.
source: As expected, we found that tamoxifen injection increased the number of starter cells expressing both GFP and mCherry in PL compared to vehicle (Figure 2C–E), confirming the specificity of these tools to restrict tracing to PL engram cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: The increase in starter cells with tamoxifen confirms the specificity of these tools to restrict tracing to PL engram cells.
source: As expected, we found that tamoxifen injection increased the number of starter cells expressing both GFP and mCherry in PL compared to vehicle (Figure 2C–E), confirming the specificity of these tools to restrict tracing to PL engram cells.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Most traced cells were found in the mPFC itself and its neighboring areas (orbitofrontal cortex, OFC, and dorsal peduncular area, DP).
source: Although most traced cells were found in the mPFC itself and its neighboring areas (orbitofrontal cortex, OFC, and dorsal peduncular area, DP, Figure 2H), we observed traced inputs in several other brain regions, notably the claustrum (CLA, Figure 2G inset 1), insular cortex (INS, inset 1), basolateral amygdala (BLA, inset 2), retrosplenial cortex (RSP, inset 3), CA1 field of the HPC (mostly the ventral part, inset 4), taenia tecta (TT), thalamus polymodal association cortex-related areas (DORpm), subiculum (SUB), and to a lesser extent the entorhinal cortex (EC, inset 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Traced inputs were observed in the claustrum (CLA), insular cortex (INS), basolateral amygdala (BLA), retrosplenial cortex (RSP), CA1 field of the HPC (mostly the ventral part), taenia tecta (TT), thalamus polymodal association cortex-related areas (DORpm), subiculum (SUB), and entorhinal cortex (EC).
source: Although most traced cells were found in the mPFC itself and its neighboring areas (orbitofrontal cortex, OFC, and dorsal peduncular area, DP, Figure 2H), we observed traced inputs in several other brain regions, notably the claustrum (CLA, Figure 2G inset 1), insular cortex (INS, inset 1), basolateral amygdala (BLA, inset 2), retrosplenial cortex (RSP, inset 3), CA1 field of the HPC (mostly the ventral part, inset 4), taenia tecta (TT), thalamus polymodal association cortex-related areas (DORpm), subiculum (SUB), and to a lesser extent the entorhinal cortex (EC, inset 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and 2H.

claim: Without tamoxifen injection, traced cells were negligible.
source: Without tamoxifen injection, traced cells were negligible (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which further confirms the rabies tracing specificity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The negligible traced cells without tamoxifen confirms the rabies tracing specificity.
source: Without tamoxifen injection, traced cells were negligible (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which further confirms the rabies tracing specificity.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: The EC was selected for further investigation because of its role in memory formation and its known projection to the mPFC necessary at encoding and retrieval.
source: Out of the regions projecting to PL engrams, we selected six brain areas with consistent input tracing for further investigation, because of their previously documented implication in various aspects of fear memory: The EC, for its role in memory formation (Roy et al., 2017) and its known projection to the mPFC necessary at encoding (Kitamura et al., 2017) and retrieval (Pilkiw et al., 2022);
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on EC function.

claim: The RSP was selected for further investigation because of its necessity for recent and remote fear memory recall.
source: the RSP for its necessity for recent (Cowansage et al., 2014) and remote fear memory recall (Todd et al., 2016);
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on RSP function.

claim: The INS was selected for further investigation because of its requirement during the consolidation and expression of contextual fear memories, as well as for its regulation of fear expression.
source: the INS for its requirement during the consolidation and expression of contextual fear memories (Alves et al., 2013), as well as for its regulation of fear expression (Gehrlach et al., 2019; Klein et al., 2021);
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on INS function.

claim: vCA1 was selected for further investigation because of its importance for CFC encoding and recent recall.
source: vCA1 for its importance for CFC encoding (Kim and Cho, 2020) and recent recall (Jimenez et al., 2020);
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on vCA1 function.

claim: The BLA was selected for further investigation because of the role of BLA to PL projections in memory encoding and PL to BLA projections in memory recall.
source: the BLA for the role of BLA to PL projections in memory encoding (Kitamura et al., 2017; Klavir et al., 2017) and PL to BLA projections in memory recall (Do-Monte et al., 2015; Kitamura et al., 2017);
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on BLA-PL connectivity.

claim: The CLA was selected for further investigation because CLA to EC projections are necessary during memory encoding and for its involvement in attention.
source: and the CLA as CLA to EC projections are necessary during memory encoding (Kitanishi and Matsuo, 2017) and for its involvement in attention (Atlan et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on CLA function.

claim: There was a significant activation of EC → PL projections at encoding compared to both recent and remote recalls.
source: In the EC, we observed a significant activation of PL projections at encoding compared to both recent and remote recalls (Figure 3E), which was not the case in total cFos quantifications (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claim: The activation of EC → PL projections at encoding was not observed in total cFos quantifications.
source: In the EC, we observed a significant activation of PL projections at encoding compared to both recent and remote recalls (Figure 3E), which was not the case in total cFos quantifications (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claim: The differential activation of EC → PL projections at encoding suggests a specific recruitment of EC neurons projecting to PL at encoding.
source: This suggests a specific recruitment of EC neurons projecting to PL (EC → PL) at encoding.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: There was no activation in RSPag → PL projections at encoding, but there was activation during recent memory recall.
source: In contrast, RSPag and INS displayed a different pattern of activation, as there was no activation in RSPag → PL and INS → PL projections at encoding, but during recent memory recall (Figure 3I and M, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: There was no activation in INS → PL projections at encoding, but there was activation during recent memory recall.
source: In contrast, RSPag and INS displayed a different pattern of activation, as there was no activation in RSPag → PL and INS → PL projections at encoding, but during recent memory recall (Figure 3I and M, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: The activity in RSPag → PL and INS → PL projections during recent recall was specific to PL projectors compared to total cFos in both regions.
source: Compared to total cFos in both regions, this activity was again specific to PL projectors (Figure 3J and N, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3J and 3N.

claim: There was no differential recruitment of vCA1 → PL projections between different times of memory consolidation.
source: In vCA1, we observed no differential recruitment of vCA1 → PL projections between different times of memory consolidation (Figure 3Q, R; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3Q, R, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The elevated cFos expression in the vCA1 as a whole at encoding as well as in the no shock group supports the role of HPC in context exploration.
source: However, the elevated cFos expression in the vCA1 as a whole at encoding as well as in the no shock group supports the role of HPC in context exploration (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B; Schiller et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Schiller et al. 2015.

claim: There was a significant activation of BLA → PL projections at encoding compared to the recalls.
source: For the BLA, we found a significant activation of BLA → PL projections at encoding compared to the recalls (Figure 3U), which is not the case for total cFos in BLA (Figure 3V).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3U and 3V.

claim: The recruitment of BLA → PL projection at encoding is in agreement with its importance during fear memory formation.
source: The recruitment of BLA → PL projection at encoding is in agreement with its importance during fear memory formation (Kitamura et al., 2017; Klavir et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on BLA-PL connectivity during memory formation.

claim: The same pattern of activation as BLA → PL was observed in CLA → PL projections.
source: Interestingly, we observed the same pattern of activation in CLA → PL projections (Figure 3Y), together with an overall higher activation of the whole CLA region at encoding compared to remote recall (Figure 3Z).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3Y and 3Z.

claim: There was an overall higher activation of the whole CLA region at encoding compared to remote recall.
source: Interestingly, we observed the same pattern of activation in CLA → PL projections (Figure 3Y), together with an overall higher activation of the whole CLA region at encoding compared to remote recall (Figure 3Z).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3Z.

claim: PL inputs from the EC, BLA, and CLA were active only at encoding, while RSPag and INS projections were recruited during recent memory recall.
source: Taken together, we found that PL inputs from the EC, BLA, and CLA were active only at encoding, while RSPag and INS projections were recruited during recent memory recall.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the experimental data on PL input activity patterns.

claim: CLA → PL inhibition during encoding resulted in impaired memory at recent recall.
source: For the CLA → PL inhibition, we observed an impaired memory at recent recall (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: CNO inhibits hM4Di-expressing neurons during behavior.
source: To confirm that CNO indeed inhibits hM4Di-expressing neurons, we expressed it in CLA → PL neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and perfused the animals 90 min after CFC to stain for cFos (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C). While the percentages of hM4Di+ and cFos+ cells were equivalent in both groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E), the amount of double positive hM4Di+cFos+ cells was significantly decreased with CNO injection, confirming the inhibition of projection neurons during behavior (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The behavioral result of CLA → PL inhibition was not due to a delayed effect of CNO injection.
source: Furthermore, this behavioral result was not due to a delayed effect of CNO injection, as inhibiting CLA → PL projections right after encoding did not result in impaired memory at any time point (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: The effect of CLA → PL inhibition was not due to an unspecific effect on locomotion and exploratory behavior.
source: Likewise, the effect of CLA → PL inhibition was not due to an unspecific effect on locomotion and exploratory behavior as tested in an open field arena (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C-E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C-E.

claim: When BLA → PL projections were inhibited during encoding, there was an impairment of remote memory recall.
source: In contrast to the effect of CLA → PL inhibition, when BLA → PL and EC → PL projections were inhibited during encoding, we observed an impairment of remote memory recall for both, while recent recall was unaffected (Figure 4H, I, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: When EC → PL projections were inhibited during encoding, there was an impairment of remote memory recall.
source: In contrast to the effect of CLA → PL inhibition, when BLA → PL and EC → PL projections were inhibited during encoding, we observed an impairment of remote memory recall for both, while recent recall was unaffected (Figure 4H, I, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: BLA → PL and EC → PL projections are important at encoding for the consolidation of remote memories.
source: These results indicate that while the BLA → PL and EC → PL projections are important at encoding for the consolidation of remote memories, as shown previously (Kitamura et al., 2017), the CLA → PL projection is important at encoding for recalling recent memories.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Kitamura et al. 2017.

claim: The CLA → PL projection is important at encoding for recalling recent memories.
source: These results indicate that while the BLA → PL and EC → PL projections are important at encoding for the consolidation of remote memories, as shown previously (Kitamura et al., 2017), the CLA → PL projection is important at encoding for recalling recent memories.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: RSPag → PL projection inhibition during recent recall did not affect memory retrieval.
source: We found that although the RSPag → PL projection was specifically active at recent recall (Figure 3I), its inhibition during this time did not affect memory retrieval (Figure 4J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: It is unlikely that the RSPag → PL projection is involved in the expression or reconsolidation of fear memories later on, as memory performance was unchanged at later times after recent recall inhibition.
source: It is also unlikely that the RSPag → PL projection is involved in the expression or reconsolidation of fear memories later on, as memory performance was unchanged at later times after recent recall inhibition (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: It is possible that the RSPag → PL projection could play a role in extinction of fear memories.
source: However, it is still possible that this projection could play a role in extinction of fear memories, which would need to be tested in future experiments.
evidence: The claim is speculative about future experiments.

claim: It is the granular subregion of the RSP and not the RSPag that is responsible for recent and remote recall.
source: Of further note, it was recently reported that although the entire RSP is necessary for recent and remote recall, it is rather the granular subregion of the RSP and not the RSPag that is responsible for this effect, suggesting a dissociated role of the two RSP subregions which could explain our observations (Tsai et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tsai et al. 2022.

claim: INS → PL projection inhibition during recent recall resulted in decreased freezing.
source: Conversely, INS → PL projection inhibition during recent recall resulted in decreased freezing (Figure 4K), positing this pathway to be important for recent fear memory expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: The INS → PL pathway is important for recent fear memory expression.
source: Conversely, INS → PL projection inhibition during recent recall resulted in decreased freezing (Figure 4K), positing this pathway to be important for recent fear memory expression.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Consistent with no significant activation of the INS → PL projection at remote memory recall, the inhibition of this projection did not result in any behavioral effect.
source: In contrast, consistent with no significant activation of the INS → PL projection at remote memory recall, the inhibition of this projection did not result in any behavioral effect (Figure 4L).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: CLA, BLA, and EC projections to the PL are required at encoding for proper memory formation, but with different time implications.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that CLA, BLA, and EC projections to the PL are required at encoding for proper memory formation, but with different time implications.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The BLA and EC connections are important for recalling remote memories.
source: While the BLA and EC connections are important for recalling remote memories, the CLA projection is specifically important for recalling recent ones.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The CLA projection is specifically important for recalling recent memories.
source: While the BLA and EC connections are important for recalling remote memories, the CLA projection is specifically important for recalling recent ones.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Recent memory recall is under the influence of the INS → PL projection.
source: In addition, recent memory recall is also under the influence of the INS → PL projection, since its inhibition at this time led to significant memory impairment.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: There is a progressive functional shift in PL projections regulating memory consolidation.
source: This suggests a progressive functional shift in PL projections regulating memory consolidation.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Engram reactivation has been correlated with memory retention in BLA.
source: Indeed, engram reactivation has been correlated with memory retention in BLA (Reijmers et al., 2007), and artificial engram reactivation in the PL (Kitamura et al., 2017) or HPC (Liu et al., 2012) has been found to trigger memory recall.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reijmers et al. 2007.

claim: Artificial engram reactivation in the PL has been found to trigger memory recall.
source: Indeed, engram reactivation has been correlated with memory retention in BLA (Reijmers et al., 2007), and artificial engram reactivation in the PL (Kitamura et al., 2017) or HPC (Liu et al., 2012) has been found to trigger memory recall.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kitamura et al. 2017.

claim: Artificial engram reactivation in the HPC has been found to trigger memory recall.
source: Indeed, engram reactivation has been correlated with memory retention in BLA (Reijmers et al., 2007), and artificial engram reactivation in the PL (Kitamura et al., 2017) or HPC (Liu et al., 2012) has been found to trigger memory recall.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al. 2012.

claim: CLA → PL inhibition during encoding confirmed the impaired memory at recent memory recall as observed in WT mice.
source: First, we focused on the CLA → PL inhibition at memory encoding (Figure 5D). Behaviorally, this approach confirmed the impaired memory at recent memory recall as observed in WT mice (Figure 5E, see also Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and comparison to Figure 4G.

claim: There was a significant correlation between PL engram cells reactivation and freezing at recent recall, which was observed only in the CNO group for CLA → PL inhibition.
source: Furthermore, we found a significant correlation between PL engram cells reactivation, measured as double positive GFP+cFos+ cells normalized to the total number of GFP+ cells, and freezing at recent recall, which was observed only in the CNO group (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: No differences were observed in overall GFP+, cFos+, double positive GFP+cFos+, and total reactivation percentages in PL between CNO- and vehicle-treated animals for CLA → PL inhibition.
source: No differences were observed in overall GFP+, cFos+, double positive GFP+cFos+, and total reactivation percentages in PL between CNO- and vehicle-treated animals. (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: When CLA → PL projection was inhibited during encoding and remote recall was tested, memory was not impaired.
source: In contrast, when we inhibited the CLA → PL projection during encoding and tested remote recall, memory was not impaired (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, see also Figure 4G) and we observed no effect on PL engram reactivation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and comparison to Figure 4G.

claim: There was no effect on PL engram reactivation when CLA → PL projection was inhibited during encoding and remote recall was tested.
source: In contrast, when we inhibited the CLA → PL projection during encoding and tested remote recall, memory was not impaired (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, see also Figure 4G) and we observed no effect on PL engram reactivation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–G.

claim: The correlation between engram reactivation and freezing was not a side effect of CNO injection.
source: Importantly, this correlation was not a side effect of CNO injection as we observed no behavioral nor engram reactivation differences in control virus-injected animals receiving vehicle or CNO (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–C.

claim: CLA → PL inhibition during encoding modifies PL engram reactivation at recent recall only.
source: This result indicates that CLA → PL inhibition during encoding modifies PL engram reactivation at recent recall only, and that following this inhibition, the less animals reactivate the original PL engram, the less they recall the fear memory.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Following CLA → PL inhibition during encoding, the less animals reactivate the original PL engram, the less they recall the fear memory.
source: This result indicates that CLA → PL inhibition during encoding modifies PL engram reactivation at recent recall only, and that following this inhibition, the less animals reactivate the original PL engram, the less they recall the fear memory.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: INS → PL inhibition at recent recall confirmed the behavioral effect on memory retrieval in WT mice.
source: Second, we inhibited the INS → PL projection at recent recall, which also confirmed the behavioral effect on memory retrieval (Figure 5H) in WT mice (Figure 4K).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H and comparison to Figure 4K.
